newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Chelsea Clinton takes centre stage on Africa tour.
newsitem.headline: Chelsea Clinton takes centre stage on Africa tour.

text.p: Chelsea Clinton on Tuesday emerged from the shadow of her mother, U.S. First Lady Hillary Rodham Clinton, for the first time on their tour of Africa -- and not surprisingly her message sounded much like mom and dad.

She spoke publicly in remote northern Tanzania, at Kilimanjaro International Airport, where Mrs. Clinton and her 17-year-old daughter were honouring a group of young women and their Peace Corps teacher for climbing Mount Kilimanjaro.
Mrs. Clinton told them that perhaps Chelsea should answer some questions from them since she also likes to hike on mountains and is closer to their age.
It was the first time Mrs. Clinton's aides could remember her giving the floor to her daughter in front of reporters, since the Clintons closely guard their Chelsea's privacy.

Chelsea talked of a "hopelessness and cynicism" that grips many American youth because of a culture of drugs and violence, and that it is up to the young people themselves to reverse this downward spiral. It is much the same sort of message often preached by President and Mrs. Clinton.
"There are a lot of problems," Chelsea told the teenaged climbers when they asked what obstacles young people face in America. "We have a big problem of violence in our country in all spectrums.
"We have a big problem with drugs, and we have a big problem with people not thinking they have a future. Young women and young men... There's a lot of hopelessness."
She said teachers and parents are trying to help stop the problem of violence and to establish a standard of equality between young women and young men.
But she said that "with our problem of hopelessness and cynicism," the biggest effort ultimately "has to come from the young people themselves."
"I think that's something we have to work on collectively as a group to try to realise that we are the future and we make of our future what we make of it," she said.

Up until now Chelsea had remained a silent partner to her mother during their goodwill tour of Africa, sometimes breaking away from serious events to have some fun of her own, like seeing prehistoric drawings in Harare, Zimbabwe.

Chelsea was also featured prominently at a visit to Olturoto Village, a poor community of the Masai people outside of Arusha at the base of Mt. Meru. The Clintons went there by riding four-wheel drive vehicles up a rutted, muddy road lined with people living a meagre existence.

The young women of the village turned out in bright tribal costumes of blue and red and gave ululations of joy at the Clintons' arrival. They draped a stiff round collar of multi- coloured beads around the necks of Chelsea and Mrs. Clinton, and Chelsea bounced up and down to the beat of their singing.
The collars are called Ushangaa in the Swahili tongue and are worn by married women and women ready for marriage, meaning they have undergone a circumcision ritual.
The Clintons watched villagers perform a skit outlining the dangers of AIDS, a disease that Tanzania estimates will afflict nearly one million Tanzanians by the year 2000.
"The children are all going to die because of AIDS," they sang.

Later, the Clintons went on what was perhaps the most anticipated part of their two-week tour of six African countries. They boarded a 19-seat prop plane and flew a half hour to a dirt landing strip, where they boarded Land Rover vehicles and drove two hours up a rocky road to a lodge overlooking the Ngorongoro Crater.
From that base, they planned to go on safari to see elephants, rhinos and lions on the crater floor as well as the nearby Serengeti Plain.
